hint: Or Elimination on the premise; each case is a contraposition, which needs Negation Introduction.
Assume the antecedent, then Or Elimination on it with p as the shared conclusion.
Nested Or Elimination. In the ¬p case there is no ex falso, so reach q ∨ r by contradiction.
Two nested conditional proofs; take the premise apart with And Elimination.
Assume the negation of the goal; under it both p and q become provable, which contradicts the premise.
Open two nested conditional proofs. Combine their assumptions before applying the premise, then discharge the inner subproof first.
Build one implication for each disjunct, both concluding q ∨ p. Then apply Or Elimination.
Prove both directions separately. And Introduction may use the same available line for both conjuncts.
Derive p ⇒ ¬p using Or Introduction. In a separate one-line subproof, assume p and discharge it to obtain p ⇒ p. Apply Negation Introduction to the two implications.
Use three nested conditional proofs. Extract both conjuncts, apply the assumed implications, and combine the results before discharging the assumptions.
Prove each direction separately. In each subproof, preserve r and use the appropriate direction of the premise to replace the other conjunct.
Assume the antecedent disjunction. Build an implication from each disjunct to r ∨ q, then use Or Elimination.
In separate subproofs, derive q and ¬q from p ∧ r. Apply Negation Introduction to the two discharged implications.
Build ¬p ⇒ r and ¬p ⇒ ¬r in separate subproofs. Negation Introduction gives ¬¬p; finish with Negation Elimination.

Prove both directions separately, then use Biconditional Introduction. For each negation, build two implications with the same antecedent and contradictory consequents, as in the chapter’s Negation Introduction strategy.
Use two nested conditional proofs. Extract both conjuncts, then apply Implication Elimination twice. Close the inner subproof before the outer one.
Build a separate implication from each disjunct to the reversed disjunction, then use Or Elimination.
Prove the two directions separately. Use the premise to build the conjunction in one direction, and And Elimination in the other.
In separate subproofs, derive implications from p ∧ q to p and to ¬p. Combine those implications with Negation Introduction.

Open three nested subproofs, assuming each antecedent in turn. Extract p and q, derive r and s, and conjoin them. Then discharge the assumptions from innermost to outermost using the chapter’s conditional-proof method.
Prove both directions separately. Starting from p, use the premise to obtain the missing conjunct. Starting from p ∧ q, extract p.
Assume p ∨ q. Within that subproof, prove two implications with consequent r ∨ q: one starting from p and one starting from q. Apply Disjunction Elimination before discharging the outer assumption.

Assume p ⇔ q in two separate subproofs. In the first, derive q using p and the forward direction of the biconditional. In the second, extract ¬q from the premise. Discharge both subproofs and apply Negation Introduction, as described in the chapter.

Prove the two directions separately. In each direction, eliminate the disjunction by constructing an implication for each disjunct. Keep the branches separate: only their discharged implications remain available afterward.
First prove p by reductio: under ¬p, construct p ⇒ q using a nested reductio for q. Then prove ¬q by showing that q would also yield p ⇒ q. Finish with And Introduction.
Use cases on p ∨ q. In each case, extract both conjuncts supplied by the corresponding premise, introduce s ∨ m, and assemble the entire goal before discharging the case.
Extract both implications from the premise. To prove p ⇒ q, assume p and construct ¬q ⇒ p; pair it with ¬q ⇒ ¬p to obtain ¬¬q. Reverse the roles of p and q for the other direction.

Assume ¬(p ∧ q), then assume the negation of the desired disjunction. Under that second assumption, prove p and q separately by reductio. Use p ∧ q and its negation as the contradictory consequents of two implications, following the chapter’s Negation Introduction pattern.
